scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9105: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports they have completely
lost connectivity to the partner network -- they cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2) in
the peer AS since this morning. The team is convinced the peer's router, router2,
dropped the peering and want router2 restarted. Please find and confirm the real
fault and tell us which device to restart.

injection.action: administratively down the inter-AS interface (eth0) on router1

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth0 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is the inter-AS link on router1: router1's eth0 (the interface to
router2) is DOWN, so the physical/L2 path between the two ASes is broken. As a
CONSEQUENCE the eBGP session between router1 and router2 drops and the inter-AS
prefixes are withdrawn, so pc1 (195.11.14.2) cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2). The
ticket MISDIRECTS to router2 ("router2 dropped the peering"), but the fault is on
the LOCAL side: it is router1's own inter-AS interface that is down. router2 is
healthy -- its bgpd is still running and its inter-AS interface is up; the session
is down only because router1's link went away.

The correct diagnosis identifies router1 (inter-AS link / eth0 down) as the root
cause and explicitly EXONERATES router2: router2's BGP daemon and interface are
fine, so the user's "router2 dropped the peering" hypothesis is wrong. An agent
that restarts / blames router2 has followed the ticket's misdirection instead of
the evidence.
scenario.fix_spec:
Bring the inter-AS link back up: on router1 run `ip link set eth0 up`. Once eth0
is up again, the eBGP session to router2 re-establishes, the inter-AS prefixes are
re-exchanged, and pc1 reaches pc2 normally. router2 needs no change -- it was
healthy the whole time.
scoring_axes: must-identify-link-down: identifies the inter-AS link (router1 eth0) is down as the root cause, with BGP loss as a consequence

bonus-notes-router2-healthy: rejects the ticket's "router2 dropped the peering" hypothesis by any valid evidence -- e.g. router2's config/daemon verified fine, its failed pings explained by the far end being down, or an explicit 'do not restart router2'

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected component is router1's eth0 interface — the physical link connecting
router1 (AS 1) to router2 (AS 2) on the 193.10.11.0/24 segment. The interface is
administratively/link-down: its flags show only <BROADCAST,MULTICAST> with no UP or
LOWER_UP, meaning the kernel has no active carrier on that interface.

Because eth0 is down, the kernel never installs the 193.10.11.0/24 connected route.
Without a path to 193.10.11.2 (router2's address), router1's BGP daemon cannot
open or sustain a TCP session to its eBGP peer. The BGP neighbor detail confirms
this explicitly: "Last reset 00:01:12, No path to specified Neighbor." The session
dropped once (Connections established 1; dropped 1) and is stuck in Active state,
retrying every 120 seconds. As a result, router1 receives no BGP updates from
router2 and its RIB contains only the one directly-connected prefix (195.11.14.0/24).
It has no route to 200.1.1.0/24 (pc2's network), so any packet from pc1 destined
for 200.1.1.2 hits router1 and triggers an ICMP Destination Net Unreachable back to
the sender — exactly the symptom reported.

Router2 is completely healthy: eth0 is UP, both prefixes are in its routing table,
and it has a live BGP session (the hold timer simply has not expired yet on its side).
Restarting router2 would have no effect whatsoever.

Root cause: router1's eth0 interface is down, removing the only path to router2 and
collapsing the eBGP session.

Corrective fix: On router1, execute `ip link set eth0 up` (or equivalent startup
config fix) to restore the link. The 193.10.11.0/24 connected route will reinstall
immediately, BGP will reconnect within the retry interval (~48 s), and router1 will
re-learn the 200.1.1.0/24 prefix from router2, restoring full pc1↔pc2 connectivity.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-link-down: identifies the inter-AS link (router1 eth0) is down as the root cause, with BGP loss as a consequence
per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly names router1's eth0 as the root cause (link down) and describes the BGP session loss as the consequent effect, exonerating router2.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-router2-healthy: rejects the ticket's "router2 dropped the peering" hypothesis by any valid evidence -- e.g. router2's config/daemon verified fine, its failed pings explained by the far end being down, or an explicit 'do not restart router2'
per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly exonerates router2, citing eth0 UP, routing/BGP state showing it is healthy, and stating that restarting router2 would have no effect.
Recommends bringing router1's eth0 up (ip link set eth0 up), which directly restores the inter‑AS link and allows the eBGP session and routes to be re-established.

The agent's logs show the key observations (eth0 down on router1, router1 BGP in Active state with 'No path to specified Neighbor', router2 BGP/interface healthy, and pc1→pc2 pings failing with ICMP Destination Net Unreachable), and the writeup correctly ties these together. The claims are well supported and the inference chain from interface down → BGP session failure → withdrawn routes → host reachability loss is logical and complete.
